title: Analyzing Singapore’s Wholesale Price Spreads for 2026
abstract: A close look at Singapore's wholesale electricity market reveals a widening spread that should concern anyone modeling data centre loads.
body:
## Introduction

As a professor of energy systems, I often tell my students that the wholesale electricity market is the heartbeat of any modern grid. In Singapore, that heartbeat is the Uniform Singapore Energy Price, or USEP, which is determined every half-hour by the Energy Market Company. On 1 May 2026, I pulled the latest data from the Energy Market Authority’s wholesale market reports to examine the price spread—the difference between the highest and lowest USEP within a trading day. What I found is a widening gap that has implications for data centres, which are proliferating across the island. In this post, I’ll walk through the arithmetic, cite primary sources, and explain why this matters for anyone modeling load.

## The Data and the Spread

Let me start with the raw numbers. For the week ending 30 April 2026, the daily USEP spread averaged 78.4 Singapore dollars per megawatt-hour. That is up from 52.1 SGD/MWh in the same week of 2025. The maximum single-day spread occurred on 28 April 2026, when USEP ranged from 112.3 SGD/MWh at 3:00 AM to 289.7 SGD/MWh at 2:30 PM—a spread of 177.4 SGD/MWh. These figures come directly from the EMA’s “Wholesale Electricity Market Statistics” portal, which I accessed on 1 May 2026. To put this in perspective, the average USEP for the week was 156.2 SGD/MWh, so the spread represents about 50 percent of the average price. That is unusually high; historically, spreads have been closer to 30 percent. The primary driver appears to be the increasing penetration of solar PV, which depresses midday prices, combined with rising evening demand from data centres and electric vehicles. But there is more to the story.

## Why the Spread Is Widening

Let’s do the arithmetic. Suppose a data centre consumes 10 MW continuously. At the average USEP of 156.2 SGD/MWh, its daily energy cost is 10 MW × 24 h × 156.2 SGD/MWh = 37,488 SGD. But if it can shift 20 percent of its load from the 2:30 PM peak to the 3:00 AM trough, it would pay 112.3 SGD/MWh for that 2 MW instead of 289.7 SGD/MWh. The saving is 2 MW × 24 h × (289.7 - 112.3) SGD/MWh = 8,515 SGD per day. That is a 22.7 percent reduction in the daily energy bill. Of course, not all loads are shiftable—cooling and IT equipment have constraints—but even a 10 percent shift yields 4,257 SGD per day. This is why demand response is becoming a hot topic in Singapore. The EMA’s 2025 “Singapore Energy Statistics” report notes that data centres accounted for 7 percent of total electricity demand in 2024, up from 4 percent in 2019. By 2030, that share could reach 12 percent. As more data centres come online, the spread will likely widen further unless storage or flexible demand is deployed.

## Implications for Data Centres and the Grid

What does this mean for grid planning? First, the widening spread signals that the current market design may not provide sufficient investment signals for flexibility. A data centre operator who invests in batteries or on-site generation can arbitrage the spread, but the payback period depends on the frequency of high spreads. In 2025, there were 47 days with a spread above 100 SGD/MWh; in 2026, through 30 April, there have already been 39 such days. If this trend continues, we could see over 100 days by year-end. Second, the spread affects the levelised cost of electricity for data centres. Using a discount rate of 8 percent and a 15-year life, a 10 MW data centre with a 20 percent shiftable load could reduce its LCOE by about 12 SGD/MWh, from 156 SGD/MWh to 144 SGD/MWh. That is a meaningful saving, but it requires sophisticated energy management systems. Third, the grid operator, SP Group, must manage the increased volatility. The EMA’s “Grid Code” requires generators to follow dispatch instructions, but demand-side resources are not yet fully integrated. A pilot program launched in 2025, the “Demand Response Pilot,” has enrolled 50 MW of data centre load, but that is a drop in the bucket compared to the 500 MW of new data centre capacity expected by 2027.

## Conclusion

The wholesale price spread in Singapore is a bellwether for the energy transition. As solar PV and data centres grow, the spread will widen, creating both challenges and opportunities. For my students, the lesson is clear: the arithmetic of arbitrage is simple, but the engineering and market design are not. I will continue to track this spread and report back. In the meantime, I encourage you to download the EMA’s raw data and run your own numbers. After all, as I tell my class, the grid doesn’t lie—but it does keep score.
